🐛 Bug
nn.ModuleList does not have meaningful semantics for forward, yet calling forward does not raise informative exceptions. I have seen this be confusing for many students in a course we are teaching. For a call to forward with non-empty arguments, instead of the apparently intended NotImplementedException or, alternatively, the default Python AttributeError ("ModuleList object has no attribute 'forward'") that one might expect, we instead get a TypeError: forward() takes 1 positional argument but <n> were given.
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

nn.ModuleList().forward() # results in expected NotImplementedException being raised
nn.ModuleList().forward(torch.zeros(1)) # results in TypeError: forward() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given

Expected behavior
nn.ModuleList().forward(*args) should raise NotImplementedException for any argument list to make it clear that forward is unsupported/unimplemented functionality for nn.ModuleList (and not merely a call with wrong arguments).
The issues is in the current implementation of the forward method, which raises NotImplementedException but takes no arguments (except self), resulting in the above issues.
Environment
The issue is independent of environment/runtime. It is present in current master and a quick look suggests that it is present at least since version 1.4.

🚀 Feature
For multi-workers dataloaders, if the persistent_workers is true, it will save about 30% training time on Windows.
It can be reproduced with
https://github.com/pytorch/examples/tree/master/mnist
https://github.com/pytorch/examples/tree/master/imagenet
Motivation
Python multiprocessing only support spawn on Windows. Starting a process using this method is rather slow compared to using fork
Windows real-time virus & thread protection will add extra 0.5~0.8 seconds of starting a process.
Even for a small imagenet dataset, it will take 16 seconds to iterate MultiPorcessingDataLoaderIter in each epoch if there're 8 workers.(https://github.com/pytorch/examples/tree/master/imagenet)
Pitch
On Windows, users can get better experience without setting persistent_workers as True explicitly.
Alternatives

Additional context
On Linux the default start method is fork, If there isn't data to be cached or requirement of tracking the dataset, it has no obvious gain with persistent workers.
From comments, we've known it would take some time to start a process, why we don't start worker processes asynchronously? Is there special concern？

🐛 Bug
The final result of running conv2d on GPU without CuDNN support (ATen) differs from that run on CPU or GPU with CuDNN support. Specifically, stride != 1 seems to be the key to the issue because the following script doesn't reveal the bug if stride = 1.
To Reproduce
The main script is as follows
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(0)

in_channels = 64
out_channels = 128
stride = 2
W = 32
H = 32

image = torch.rand(1, in_channels, W, H)
net = nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=1, stride=stride, bias=False)
torch.save(net, '.\model.pkl')

def runcpu(image):
    net = torch.load('.\model.pkl')
    net.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():        
        output = net(image)
    return output

def runCuDNN(image):
    net = torch.load('.\model.pkl').cuda()
    net.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():        
        torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = True
        output = net(image.cuda())
    return output

def runNoCuDNN(image):
    net = torch.load('.\model.pkl').cuda()
    net.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():        
        torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False
        output = net(image.cuda())
    return output


noCuDNN_output = runNoCuDNN(image)
cpu_output = runcpu(image)
CuDNN_output = runCuDNN(image)
print(cpu_output.sum())
print(CuDNN_output.sum())
print(noCuDNN_output.sum())

Here I use torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False to disable CuDNN.
The result is
tensor(502.4232)
tensor(502.4232, device='cuda:0')
tensor(541.0007, device='cuda:0')

Expected behavior
The output shows that the results of runcpu and runCuDNN are consistent, while runNoCuDNN is greatly different from them. It is expected that different running backends should produce exactly the same results. Note that stride != 1 seems to be the key to the issue because the above script doesn't reveal the bug if stride = 1.

GlooStore and Store APIs are inconsistent
ProcessGroupGloo wraps Store in a GlooStore, which has the following wait API signature (sets a std::vector<char>):
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/lib/c10d/ProcessGroupGloo.cpp#L175
However, Store has the following signature (sets a std::vector<uint8_t>):
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/lib/c10d/Store.hpp#L29
This results in having to write different code when using GlooStore/Store, but ideally user wouldn't even need to be aware of the underlying store impl and the code would be simplified if both had the same interface. We would also be able to remove some code that is responsible for converting std::vector<char> -> std::vector<uint8_t> and vice versa.

Hi, I've been doing some benchmarking with various implementations of transformers on language modeling, and I noticed that the specifics of your transformer implementation/initialization make it unstable when training deeper 12+ layer transformers.
There are two main variants of transformers, post and pre norm (this basically just has to do with where the layer norms are placed, but it's an important distinction for training stability, see this presentation).
You guys use post norm. This is ok, but it doesn't work on deeper transformers with the specific Xavier-uniform initialization you use. Let me explain:
Both pre- and post-norm perform similarly when tuned. Pre-norm usually works with most generic initializations and doesn't usually require LR-warmup to get decent performance. Post-norm, on the other hand, is usually hard to train for deeper networks (12+ layers), it requires precise initialization and a good LR schedule; this is because putting the layer norm after the residual causes each layer's Jacobian singular values to not be closely distributed around 1, which causes vanishing gradients (see figure 5 of this paper). With the right initialization, this issue can be overcome, but the specific initialization you guys use does not fix this at all.
In fact for deeper transformers, using the kaiming-uniform initialization (this is the default for Linear layers) is much better than the custom Xavier-uniform initialization you are using.
To prove this I've run some experiments. If you train a language model with the GPT-3-small architecture hyper-parameters (this has 12 transformer layers) on wiki-text-103, the validation cross-entropy will basically flatline at about 7 after approx. one-hundred iterations of training. On the other hand if you commit out line 66 of pytorch/torch/nn/modules/transformer.py – self._reset_parameters() – the model will actually train for several epochs before converging at around 3.6 validation cross-entropy.
I've attached plots of the training and validation loss for these experiments below (NOTE: the runs labeled with pytorch are from your transformer implementation, the ones labeled with custom are from my own implementation; I cut some of the runs short because I didn't have time, but I let one run from my own custom implementation run for much longer, the pytorch ones track my own very closely, so they should converge similarly. Xavier-uniform is what your implementation is currently set to, kaiming-uniform is the initialization you get from commenting out just one line of your code)


To fix this there are two things you could do: either change your current default initialization scheme or switch to a pre-norm transformer. I recommend the pre-norm route since its more stable to train in general. Or you could make it an input parameter, so that users can choose which version (pre- or post- norm) they want to use. I'd actually be down to make this fix; I can make the changes and then submit a pull request, I just wanted to see what you think first. What was your thinking when implementing this ? It looks like you just went off the Attention Is All You Need paper, which is maybe a little old now.
Also just in general, I feel like there could be better abstractions for transformers; most researchers don't even use these transformer building blocks you have, instead they just use their own implementation or something else (this is in contrast to your conv-net building blocks, which are easy to work with and pretty flexible and widely used. Maybe its just cause transformers haven't had as much time to mature as conv-nets idk). I don't think any framework gets this right though. Anyways, this is a much bigger question, idk if you want to look into this or if you are already working on this, but I thought I would bring it up.
(P.S. one more thing, because you use post-norm, I think the extra norm you apply after all the layers in the TransformerEncoder/Decoder modules is redundant; this would be necessary if you were using pre-norm though)

🚀 Feature
Extend Pipeline API to support

Multi-process/multi-host setting
More flexible connections between layers.
Automatic placement of layers

Terminology

A layer is a single module in the model that has to be placed entirely on a single device. So if a part of the module is sharded, a layer here refers to individual shards (or parts of individual shard)
A partition is a group of layers that are put together into a single device and scheduled atomically by pipeline implementation.

Overview
With this proposal a pipeline model is authored in following steps

The user provides description of each layer in the model (in the form of module class and constructor parameters). Additional metadata may also be required (e.g. for automatic placement). The user also provides information how different layers are connected to each other. In the simplest form, layers have single input/output and are connected sequentially.
The user assigns layers to different devices (local or remote). Assignment could be done manually by user or by using provided helper utilities.
A pipeline scheduler class takes in these information and runs the module efficiently.

Details
Layers Definition
We would like to use existing RemoteModule implementation to let user describe individual layers in the model.
linear_layer_1 = RemoteModule("worker1/cuda:0", nn.Linear, (4, 10), {}), 
rlu_layer = RemoteModule("worker1/cuda:0", nn.ReLU, (), {})]
linear_layer_2 = RemoteModule("worker2/cuda:1", nn.Linear, (10, 1000), {}), 

In order to allow separation of layers description and placement, we need to extend RemoteModule to allow for deferred placement:
layers = [
  RemoteModule(None, nn.Linear, (4, 10), {}), 
  RemoteModule(None, nn.ReLU, (), {})]
  RemoteModule(None, nn.Linear, (10, 1000), {})
]  

sequential_placement(layers, ["worker1/cuda:0", "worker2/cuda:1"], balance=[2, 1])

Connections
We provide API for user to define connections between layers. This let’s user to cover various scenarios, to name some:

a simple sequence of layers where each layer feeds its output to the next layer in sequence
skip connections
sharded modules, as an example:


The API is in the form of a class PipelineModulesGraph  that is instantiated by the user

class PipelineModulesGraph(nn.Module):
    def add_sequence(self, modules: List[RemoteModule]) -> None:
        ...
    def add_multi_input_layer(self,
                              module: RemoteModule,
                              inputs: List[RemoteModule]) -> None:
        ...
                            
    def feed_model_input(self, module: RemoteModule) -> None:
        ....
       

A graph defined this way is a module can run layers on given input (but not in an efficient way).
DistributedPipeline
DistributedPipeline is a wrapper module around PipelineModulesGraph that can run the underlaying pipeline-module-graph with pipelining technique. The API is similar to existing Pipe class, with the difference that the constructor accepts an instance of the more general PipelineModulesGraph class instead of nn.Sequential.

excerpts from torch/testing/__init__.py:
_floating_types = _dispatch_dtypes((torch.float32, torch.float64))
_integral_types = _dispatch_dtypes((torch.uint8, torch.int8, torch.int16, torch.int32, torch.int64))
...
_all_types = _floating_types + _integral_types
def all_types():
    return _all_types
The problem is that all_types() doesn't return all types, e.g. it misses complex types, bools, etc.
Even more confusingly, there is also get_all_dtypes() which seems to do the right thing.
I understand that these names were chosen to match the various AT_DISPATCH_* macros, but I seem to understand that we are promoting the usage of torch.testing to the general public, and these are all public functions defined in its __init__.py.
Possible solutions:

move them to torch.testing._internal. A quick grep reveals that they are used only there
take it as an opportunity to do a broader renaming of names, including ATen C++ files. E.g., what is now called all_types should called default_types or something similar
ignore the problem and maybe document the behavior, although IMHO it's very confusing
fix the names in torch.testing without fixing ATen. This is probably the worst solution as it will be very confusing for contributors and probably lead to bugs and/or missing tests

When operating on the tensor that can be viewed with requested sizes without moving memory, view and reshape functions are doing the same thing and should take the same time. Yet reshape takes much longer, because it computes the necessary strides twice (once in reshape itself, once in view), and redispatches to view for additional penalty.
To reproduce
code

import timeit

import torch
from torch.utils.benchmark import Measurement, Timer

def make_timer_view():
    return Timer("x.view(-1);", setup="at::Tensor x=torch::empty({2,2} ); ", language="c++", timer=timeit.default_timer)

def make_timer_reshape():
    return Timer("x.reshape(-1);", setup="at::Tensor x=torch::empty({2,2} ); ", language="c++", timer=timeit.default_timer)


def measure_main(fn_make_timer):
    timer = fn_make_timer()
    counts = timer.collect_callgrind(number=20, repeats=5, collect_baseline=False)
    times = timer.blocked_autorange(min_run_time=5)
    return counts, times



def main(**kwargs):

    times = [[], []]
    counts = [[], []]
    c, t = measure_main(make_timer_view)
    times[0].append(t)
    counts[0].append(c)
    c, t = measure_main(make_timer_reshape)
    times[1].append(t)
    counts[1].append(c)

    print()

    t0 = times[0]
    t1 = times[1]
    
    # Take the min as any interpreter jitter will increase from the baseline.
    c0 = min(counts[0][0], key=lambda x: x.counts(denoise=True))
    c1 = min(counts[1][0], key=lambda x: x.counts(denoise=True))

    torch.set_printoptions(linewidth=200)
    delta = (
        c1.as_standardized().stats() -
        c0.as_standardized().stats()
    ).denoise()

    print(t0, "\n")
    print(t1, "\n")
    print(c0.counts(denoise=True))
    print(c1.counts(denoise=True), "\n")
    print(delta)

    # Uncomment to debug:
    # import pdb
    # pdb.set_trace()




if __name__ == "__main__":

🚀 Feature
DLPack is a mechanism to exchange data with other tensor/array libraries. PyTorch currently has DLPack support in torch.utils.dlpack, with from_dlpack and to_dlpack functions. The implementation lives in:

torch/csrc/Module.cpp#L356
aten/src/ATen/dlpack.h

It is only at version 0.1.0 in PyTorch. This feature request is for upgrading to the latest DLPack and supporting the new Python API for it.
Motivation
DLPack is being adopted as the array API standard data interchange mechanism, see https://data-apis.org/array-api/latest/design_topics/data_interchange.html. A good motivation for why DLPack is the best protocol for that purpose, and an overview of other libraries supporting it, is given in data-apis/consortium-feedback#1.
The tl;dr is: currently there is no single protocol that is supported by all major array/tensor libraries. DLPack is meant to be that. NumPy will also adopt it; CuPy, JAX, TensorFlow, MXNet all support it too; they all need to update to v0.4.0 and the new Python API.
Upgrading to the latest DLPack will give bfloat16 and complex dtype support, and probably other improvements too (latest nontrivial commit to dlpack.h in PyTorch was in 2017).
The new Python API will have stream support, which is useful new functionality for CUDA/ROCm. There's a long design discussion at dmlc/dlpack#57, and a summary of the outcome at https://data-apis.org/array-api/latest/design_topics/data_interchange.html#semantics.
Finally, DLPack is used in production already, for example spaCy relies on it to interoperate with both PyTorch and CuPy (documented here) - so improving its support makes sense.
Pitch
I propose to:

upgrade to latest DLPack (0.4.0)
adopt the new Python API for DLPack from the array API standard:

add __dlpack__(self, stream=None) and __dlpack_device__(self) methods on torch.Tensor
add torch.from_dlpack(input, /). Note that it takes tensor-like objects with __dlpack__ and __dlpack_device__ methods, not a PyCapsule like torch.utils.dlpack.from_dlpack.


add better tests. the current implementation has only one trivial roundtrip test.

One thing that needs checking is ABI compatibility - I believe DLPack has been stable since at least v0.2.0 till v0.4.0 (latest), however PyTorch is still at v0.1.0 now. If there was an ABI break, we may have to leave the code supporting torch.utils.dlpack untouched, and introduce a new dlpack.h next to it.
Another thing that needs checking is how to resolve the issue that seems to plague the Tensor.__array__ implementation when modifying the underlying storage of an exported buffer (see 
  
    
      pytorch/torch/csrc/utils/tensor_numpy.cpp
    
    
         Line 146
      in
      f71a0da
    
  
  
    

        
          
           // TODO: This attempts to keep the underlying memory alive by setting the base 
        
    
  

).
Alternatives
There's a discussion in https://data-apis.org/array-api/latest/design_topics/data_interchange.html about why alternative data exchange protocols are falling short.
Additional context
DLPack is one feature of the array API standard; the discussion about adopting the full standard is gh-54581.
Cc @leofang, @tqchen, @emcastillo, @kmaehashi
cc @mruberry @rgommers @heitorschueroff

🐛 Bug

The code of bug report is based on the tutorial on pipeline parallelism.

When partitioning a transformer into different numbers of partitions, outputs are different.
When using different chunks of pipe, outputs are different.

To Reproduce
Used code:

change the targets.cuda(1) in L353 and L385 to targets.cuda(num_gpus - 1)
setup the random seed in L48

import random
import os

seed = 0
random.seed(seed)
np.random.seed(seed)
torch.manual_seed(seed)
torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True
torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False
os.environ["PYTHONHASHSEED"] = str(seed)

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

use different num_gpus (such as 1, 2, 4) and output logs are different. However, if we fix the num_gpus and run the code twice, the results are reproducible.
use different chunks and output logs are also different.


import sys
import math
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import tempfile
from torch.nn import TransformerEncoder, TransformerEncoderLayer

import numpy as np
import random
import os

seed = 0
random.seed(seed)
np.random.seed(seed)
torch.manual_seed(seed)
torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True
torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False
os.environ["PYTHONHASHSEED"] = str(seed)

if sys.platform == "win32":
    print("Windows platform is not supported for pipeline parallelism")
    sys.exit(0)
if torch.cuda.device_count() < 2:
    print("Need at least two GPU devices for this tutorial")
    sys.exit(0)


class Encoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, ntoken, ninp, dropout=0.5):
        super(Encoder, self).__init__()
        self.src_mask = None
        self.pos_encoder = PositionalEncoding(ninp, dropout)
        self.encoder = nn.Embedding(ntoken, ninp)
        self.ninp = ninp
        self.init_weights()

    def init_weights(self):
        initrange = 0.1
        self.encoder.weight.data.uniform_(-initrange, initrange)

    def _generate_square_subsequent_mask(self, sz):
        mask = (torch.triu(torch.ones(sz, sz)) == 1).transpose(0, 1)
        mask = (
            mask.float()
            .masked_fill(mask == 0, float("-inf"))
            .masked_fill(mask == 1, float(0.0))
        )
        return mask

    def forward(self, src):
        if self.src_mask is None or self.src_mask.size(0) != src.size(0):
            device = src.device
            mask = self._generate_square_subsequent_mask(src.size(0)).to(device)
            self.src_mask = mask

        src = self.encoder(src) * math.sqrt(self.ninp)
        return self.pos_encoder(src)


class Decoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, ntoken, ninp):
        super(Decoder, self).__init__()
        self.decoder = nn.Linear(ninp, ntoken)
        self.init_weights()

    def init_weights(self):
        initrange = 0.1
        self.decoder.bias.data.zero_()
        self.decoder.weight.data.uniform_(-initrange, initrange)

    def forward(self, inp):
        return self.decoder(inp)


class PositionalEncoding(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, dropout=0.1, max_len=5000):
        super(PositionalEncoding, self).__init__()
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(p=dropout)

        pe = torch.zeros(max_len, d_model)
        position = torch.arange(0, max_len, dtype=torch.float).unsqueeze(1)
        div_term = torch.exp(
            torch.arange(0, d_model, 2).float() * (-math.log(10000.0) / d_model)
        )
        pe[:, 0::2] = torch.sin(position * div_term)
        pe[:, 1::2] = torch.cos(position * div_term)
        pe = pe.unsqueeze(0).transpose(0, 1)
        self.register_buffer("pe", pe)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.pe[: x.size(0), :]
        return self.dropout(x)


import io
import torch
from torchtext.utils import download_from_url, extract_archive
from torchtext.data.utils import get_tokenizer
from torchtext.vocab import build_vocab_from_iterator

url = "https://s3.amazonaws.com/research.metamind.io/wikitext/wikitext-2-v1.zip"
test_filepath, valid_filepath, train_filepath = extract_archive(download_from_url(url))
tokenizer = get_tokenizer("basic_english")
vocab = build_vocab_from_iterator(
    map(tokenizer, iter(io.open(train_filepath, encoding="utf8")))
)


def data_process(raw_text_iter):
    data = [
        torch.tensor([vocab[token] for token in tokenizer(item)], dtype=torch.long)
        for item in raw_text_iter
    ]
    return torch.cat(tuple(filter(lambda t: t.numel() > 0, data)))


train_data = data_process(iter(io.open(train_filepath, encoding="utf8")))
val_data = data_process(iter(io.open(valid_filepath, encoding="utf8")))
test_data = data_process(iter(io.open(test_filepath, encoding="utf8")))

device = torch.device("cuda")


def batchify(data, bsz):
    # Divide the dataset into bsz parts.
    nbatch = data.size(0) // bsz
    # Trim off any extra elements that wouldn't cleanly fit (remainders).
    data = data.narrow(0, 0, nbatch * bsz)
    # Evenly divide the data across the bsz batches.
    data = data.view(bsz, -1).t().contiguous()
    return data.to(device)


batch_size = 20
eval_batch_size = 10
train_data = batchify(train_data, batch_size)
val_data = batchify(val_data, eval_batch_size)
test_data = batchify(test_data, eval_batch_size)


bptt = 35


def get_batch(source, i):
    seq_len = min(bptt, len(source) - 1 - i)
    data = source[i : i + seq_len]
    target = source[i + 1 : i + 1 + seq_len].view(-1)
    return data, target


ntokens = len(vocab.stoi)  # the size of vocabulary
emsize = 4096  # embedding dimension
nhid = 4096  # the dimension of the feedforward network model in nn.TransformerEncoder
nlayers = 12  # the number of nn.TransformerEncoderLayer in nn.TransformerEncoder
nhead = 16  # the number of heads in the multiheadattention models
dropout = 0.2  # the dropout value

from torch.distributed import rpc

tmpfile = tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile()
rpc.init_rpc(
    name="worker",
    rank=0,
    world_size=1,
    rpc_backend_options=rpc.TensorPipeRpcBackendOptions(
        init_method="file://{}".format(tmpfile.name),
        # Specifying _transports and _channels is a workaround and we no longer
        # will have to specify _transports and _channels for PyTorch
        # versions >= 1.8.1
        _transports=["ibv", "uv"],
        _channels=["cuda_ipc", "cuda_basic"],
    ),
)

num_gpus = 2
partition_len = ((nlayers - 1) // num_gpus) + 1

# Add encoder in the beginning.
tmp_list = [Encoder(ntokens, emsize, dropout).cuda(0)]
module_list = []

# Add all the necessary transformer blocks.
for i in range(nlayers):
    transformer_block = TransformerEncoderLayer(emsize, nhead, nhid, dropout)
    if i != 0 and i % (partition_len) == 0:
        module_list.append(nn.Sequential(*tmp_list))
        tmp_list = []
    device = i // (partition_len)
    tmp_list.append(transformer_block.to(device))

# Add decoder in the end.
tmp_list.append(Decoder(ntokens, emsize).cuda(num_gpus - 1))
module_list.append(nn.Sequential(*tmp_list))

from torch.distributed.pipeline.sync import Pipe

# Build the pipeline.
model = Pipe(torch.nn.Sequential(*module_list), chunks=8)


def get_total_params(module: torch.nn.Module):
    total_params = 0
    for param in module.parameters():
        total_params += param.numel()
    return total_params


print("Total parameters in model: {:,}".format(get_total_params(model)))


criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
lr = 5.0  # learning rate
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.StepLR(optimizer, 1.0, gamma=0.95)

import time


def train():
    model.train()  # Turn on the train mode
    total_loss = 0.0
    start_time = time.time()
    ntokens = len(vocab.stoi)

    # Train only for 50 batches to keep script execution time low.
    nbatches = min(50 * bptt, train_data.size(0) - 1)

    for batch, i in enumerate(range(0, nbatches, bptt)):
        data, targets = get_batch(train_data, i)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        # Since the Pipe is only within a single host and process the ``RRef``
        # returned by forward method is local to this node and can simply
        # retrieved via ``RRef.local_value()``.
        output = model(data).local_value()
        # Need to move targets to the device where the output of the
        # pipeline resides.
        loss = criterion(output.view(-1, ntokens), targets.cuda(num_gpus - 1))
        loss.backward()
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 0.5)
        optimizer.step()

        total_loss += loss.item()
        log_interval = 1
        if batch % log_interval == 0 and batch > 0:
            cur_loss = total_loss / log_interval
            elapsed = time.time() - start_time
            print(
                "| epoch {:3d} | {:5d}/{:5d} batches | "
                "lr {:02.2f} | ms/batch {:5.2f} | "
                "loss {:5.2f} | ppl {:8.2f}".format(
                    epoch,
                    batch,
                    nbatches // bptt,
                    scheduler.get_lr()[0],
                    elapsed * 1000 / log_interval,
                    cur_loss,
                    math.exp(cur_loss),
                )
            )
            total_loss = 0
            start_time = time.time()


def evaluate(eval_model, data_source):
    eval_model.eval()  # Turn on the evaluation mode
    total_loss = 0.0
    ntokens = len(vocab.stoi)
    # Evaluate only for 50 batches to keep script execution time low.
    nbatches = min(50 * bptt, data_source.size(0) - 1)
    with torch.no_grad():
        for i in range(0, nbatches, bptt):
            data, targets = get_batch(data_source, i)
            output = eval_model(data).local_value()
            output_flat = output.view(-1, ntokens)
            # Need to move targets to the device where the output of the
            # pipeline resides.
            total_loss += (
                len(data) * criterion(output_flat, targets.cuda(num_gpus - 1)).item()
            )
    return total_loss / (len(data_source) - 1)


best_val_loss = float("inf")
epochs = 3  # The number of epochs
best_model = None

for epoch in range(1, epochs + 1):
    epoch_start_time = time.time()
    train()
    val_loss = evaluate(model, val_data)
    print("-" * 89)
    print(
        "| end of epoch {:3d} | time: {:5.2f}s | valid loss {:5.2f} | "
        "valid ppl {:8.2f}".format(
            epoch, (time.time() - epoch_start_time), val_loss, math.exp(val_loss)
        )
    )
    print("-" * 89)

    if val_loss < best_val_loss:
        best_val_loss = val_loss
        best_model = model

    scheduler.step()


test_loss = evaluate(best_model, test_data)
print("=" * 89)
print(
    "| End of training | test loss {:5.2f} | test ppl {:8.2f}".format(
        test_loss, math.exp(test_loss)
    )
)
print("=" * 89)

Because the sync pipeline parallelism doesn't affect the parameter update, output logs should be the same no matter we modify the num_gpus / chunks or not.

🚀 Feature
Exporting PyTorch models to ONNX and guaranteeing that each operator takes at most 32bits as input/output while following the onnx spec.
Motivation
I'm trying to run an onnx model in the browser that's developed in PyTorch. JavaScript doesn't support int64. The PyTorch model is developed using float32. The problem arises when exporting to onnx. PyTorch uses int64 as default to export onnx models and the exporter adds additional operators which are int64. Some of those operators can be casted to int32 using a simple script and changing the data_type of those operators, but this can't be done for all operators. Doing so breaks the model, because following the onnx spec those operators don't have a 32bit implementation. It would be really handy if we could tell the PyTorch exporter to export the model to onnx, following the onnx spec and guaranteeing 32bits at the same time. If such a model can't be exported to a 32bit onnx model, we should get an error explaining why.
ONXX is a great idea for interoperability of ML models between platforms/frameworks, but it's not really straightforward. It works sometimes, but not always.

Following the discussion in #54002
I'd be keen on helping improving the documentation of torch.linalg and the related functions in torch.*. I'd like to correct several errata that appear here and there, make the formatting uniform and add some extra information for when the backward of the operations succeeds and when it fails.
To summarise the state of affairs. There are five ways of writing code / maths in Sphinx:

Single backticks: `A` is rendered as A
Double backticks: ``A`` is rendered as A
Attr: :attr:`A` is rendered as A
LaTeX: :math:`A` is rendered as a LaTeX image of A
Plain text: A

On top of this, the signature of the function is rendered with a different format bold letters with the arguments in italics:

As discussed in  #54002, given that the LaTeX font is completely different to the normal HTML font, it is reasonable to keep the LaTeX usage to a minimum. In particular, prefer unicode maths (see this page) over LaTeX for inline formulas. For large formulas, use the environment .. math:: which puts the formula on its own line.
It looked like everyone also agreed that :attr: was a good decorator to use when referring to input parameters.
Given these premises, the standing issue was: when do we use single backticks or double backticks?
Single backticks have the problem that introduce a new format (italics) when just one formatting (the one from double backticks and :attr: could do)
Double backticks have the problem that they are not rendered properly when the formula has spaces. See for example in torch.linalg.choleski:

How should we go about this?
In my opinion, I would go with "always use double backticks" for uniformity, as their format matches that of :attr:. We then would have to look into the spacing problem, but I guess that should be solved from within the sphinx template. Note also that these breaks just happen when the background is white. When it is not (e.g. in a note or warning) they are rendered correctly. See torch.linalg.slogdet
